newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: World Bank says resumes financial aid to Zimbabwe.
newsitem.headline: World Bank says resumes financial aid to Zimbabwe.

text.p: The World Bank said on Thursday it was resuming crucial balance-of-payments support to Zimbabwe, two years after withholding such aid over the southern African state's failure to meet some cost-cutting measures.

It invited other Western donors to follow its lead, and said the bank, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the donors would meet Zimbabwean officials in early 1998 to discuss support for a new reform programme.

The bank's deputy representative to Zimbabwe Kapil Kapoor told a news conference that the bank "has now advised (the Zimbabwe) government that senior management has approved the release of the second tranche of the second structural adjustment credit worth about $62.5 million".

Kapoor said the bank reached the decision last week after reviewing Zimbabwe's macroeconomic performance and its 18-month 1997/98 budget presented on July 24, but only communicated the decision to President Robert Mugabe's government on Wednesday.

"The release of the second tranche had been delayed as a result of macroeconomic uncertainity caused by the fiscal situation. The bank is now of the opinion that good progress has been made in turning the fiscal situation around," he said.
There was no immediate comment from the government or Zimbabwe's financial markets which were closed by the time the decision was announced.
Kapoor said he hoped other Western donors who had withheld balance-of-payments aid in 1995 over the same reasons would also now release the money.

World Bank chief representative in Harare David Cook told Reuters last month that on the face of it Zimbabwe's latest budget -- which contained a surprise reduction in the government's spending deficit -- looked good for the release of the $62.5 million balance-of-payments support and general financial aid.

In his budget statement, Finance Minister Herbert Murerwa announced an unexpected reduction in the government's spending deficit for the 1996/97 financial year ended June 30 to 7.1 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
This not only met but was also lower -- for the first time in seven years -- than the government-set target of 8.5 percent.

The government had consistently missed annual targets to whittle down the budget deficit and this was one of the factors which led the World Bank and other Western donors to suspend balance-of-payments support.

Kapoor said the World Bank was particularly heartened by the fact that the Zimbabwean government had managed to turn around the financial situation of its 10 major public enterprises under a commercialisation programme.
He said the 10 enterprises' consolidated deficit fell to 0.2 percent of GDP in 1996/97 from 3.3 percent in 1993/94 and the government was now privatising some of them at a fast rate.

"The second tranche would provide the government with much needed budgetary support which would assist government's fiscal reform efforts," he said, giving a list that included further trade liberalisation, agricultural reform, investment deregulation and commercialisation.

"While other donors would need to conduct their own independent evaluation of recent macroeconomic developments we feel this is probably an appropriate time for them to release their pending balance-of-payments support," Kapoor said.
He estimated the withheld funds at around $30 million.
